title: Ab urbe condita
author: Livy
source: Translated by Claude from phi0914.phi001.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Servius cum trabea et lictoribus prodit ac sede regia sedens alia decernit, de aliis consulturum se regem esse simulat. itaque per aliquot dies, cum iam expirasset Tarquinius, celata morte per speciem alienae fungendae vicis suas opes firmavit.
passages.english: Servius comes out in the *trabea* [the striped royal robe] and with the lictors, and, sitting on the royal seat, decides some matters and pretends that he will consult the king about others. So for several days, though Tarquinius had already died, he concealed the death and, under the appearance of discharging another's office, strengthened his own power.

passages.original: a quo facessere iussa ex tanto tumultu cum se domum reciperet pervenissetque ad summum Cyprium vicum, ubi Dianium nuper fuit, flectenti carpentum dextra in Urbium clivum, ut in collem Esquiliarum eveheretur, restitit pavidus atque inhibuit frenos is, qui iumenta agebat, iacentemque dominae Servium trucidatum ostendit.
passages.english: Ordered by him to withdraw from so great a tumult, she was returning home and had reached the top of the Cyprian Street, where the shrine of Diana was until recently; as she was turning the carriage to the right into the Urbian Slope, to be driven up onto the Esquiline hill, the man who was driving the animals stopped in terror, pulled up the reins, and showed his mistress Servius lying slaughtered.
passages.notes: "Urbium clivum": the Clivus Urbius (or Virbius), the reading is variously given in manuscripts.

passages.original: ludi quam amplissimi ut fierent, senatus decrevit. ad eos ludos auctore Attio Tullio vis magna Volscorum venit.
passages.english: The senate decreed that the games should be held on the grandest possible scale. At the instigation of Attius Tullius a great number of Volscians came to those games.

passages.original: secundum Hieronymi caedem primo tumultuatum in Leontinis apud milites fuerat vociferatumque ferociter parentandum regi sanguine coniuratorum esse.
passages.english: After the murder of Hieronymus there had at first been an uproar among the soldiers at Leontini, and they had fiercely shouted that the king's shade must be appeased with the blood of the conspirators.
passages.notes: "parentandum" refers to offering funeral rites to the dead; here, avenging the king by the conspirators' blood.

passages.original: prima forte signa sescentorum Cretensium erant, qui apud Hieronymum meruerant sub eis et Hannibalis beneficium habebant, capti ad Trasumennum inter Romanorum auxilia dimissique.
passages.english: By chance the foremost standards were those of six hundred Cretans, who had served under Hieronymus among those [troops] and were under obligation to Hannibal for a kindness, having been captured at Trasimene among the auxiliaries of the Romans and released.
passages.notes: "sub eis" is awkward; it may refer to the officers or units just mentioned in the lost preceding context.

passages.original: cautior tamen quam promptior hic habitus; et sicut dubites, utrum ingenio cunctator fuerit an quia ita bello proprie, quod tum gerebatur, aptum erat, sic nihil certius est quam unum hominem nobis cunctando rem restituisse, sicut Ennius ait.
passages.english: He was, however, considered more cautious than enterprising; and just as you might be in doubt whether he was a delayer by nature or because that suited the war then being waged in particular, so nothing is more certain than that one man by delaying restored our state, as Ennius says.

passages.original: hunc regem in triumpho ductum Polybius, haudquaquam spernendus auctor, tradit. secutus Scipionem triumphantem est pilleo capiti inposito Q. Terentius Culleo, omnique deinde vita, ut dignum erat, libertatis auctorem coluit.
passages.english: Polybius, by no means an authority to be despised, records that this king was led in the triumph. Quintus Terentius Culleo followed Scipio in his triumph with a freedman's cap set on his head, and for the whole of his life thereafter, as was fitting, he honoured [Scipio] as the author of his freedom.

passages.original: multitudinis eorum argumentum sit, quod Polybius scribit centum talentis eam rem Achaeis stetisse, cum quingenos denarios pretium in capita, quod redderetur dominis, statuissent. mille enim ducentos ea ratione Achaia habuit.
passages.english: Let it be evidence of their number that Polybius writes that this matter cost the Achaeans a hundred talents, since they had fixed a price of five hundred denarii a head, to be paid back to the owners. For on that reckoning Achaea had twelve hundred [of them].
passages.notes: Refers to Roman captives sold as slaves in Greece and ransomed by the Achaeans.

passages.original: quos Polybio auctore traiecisse secum regem in Graeciam scripsimus, exiguus numerus; quid, si Antiati Valerio credamus sexaginta milia militum fuisse in regio exercitu scribenti, quadraginta inde milia cecidisse, supra quinque milia capta cum signis militaribus ducentis triginta?
passages.english: Those whom, on Polybius' authority, we have written that the king took across with him into Greece are a small number; what if we were to believe Valerius Antias, who writes that there were sixty thousand soldiers in the royal army, that forty thousand of them fell, and that over five thousand were captured, together with two hundred and thirty military standards?

passages.original: “quando ergo” inquit “ita permittitis, postulo, ut mihi Dicaearchum civem vestrum et Menestam Epirotam” — Naupactum is cum praesidio ingressus ad defectionem compulerat — “et Amynandrum cum principibus Athamanum, quorum consilio ab nobis defecistis, sine mora dedatis.”
passages.english: "Since, then," he said, "you leave it to me in this way, I demand that you hand over to me without delay Dicaearchus, your citizen, and Menestas the Epirote" — he had entered Naupactus with a garrison and driven it to revolt — "and Amynander with the leading men of the Athamanians, on whose advice you revolted from us."

passages.original: non de accusatore convenit: alii M. Naevium, alii Petillios diem dixisse scribunt, non de tempore, quo dicta dies sit, non de anno, quo mortuus sit,
passages.english: There is no agreement about the accuser: some write that Marcus Naevius, others that the Petillii, set the day [of trial]; nor about the time when the day was set, nor about the year in which he died,
passages.notes: The sentence breaks off mid-way; the passage ends with a comma.

passages.original: Scipionem et Polybius et Rutilius hoc anno mortuum scribunt. ego neque his neque Valerio adsentior, his, quod censoribus M. Porcio L. Valerio L. Valerium principem senatus ipsum censorem lectum invenio, cum superioribus duobus lustris Africanus fuisset,
passages.english: Both Polybius and Rutilius write that Scipio died in this year. I agree neither with them nor with Valerius: with them, because I find that when Marcus Porcius and Lucius Valerius were censors, Lucius Valerius, the censor himself, was chosen as leader of the senate, although Africanus had been [leader] in the two preceding lustra,
